lessons.title: Segment Tree Structure And Build
lessons.objective: Understand the segment tree as a binary tree stored in an array, derive the 4n size requirement, and implement the build operation in O(n).
concepts: Segment tree: binary tree where each node stores aggregate of a range
Array representation: root at index 1, left child = 2*i, right child = 2*i+1
Leaf nodes store individual elements; internal nodes store aggregates
Build: recursively compute aggregates bottom-up from leaves
Why 4n size: worst case when n is not a power of 2
O(n) build: each of the 2n-1 nodes computed exactly once
Supports: range sum, range min, range max, range GCD
The aggregate function must be associative (but not necessarily commutative)
lessons.explanation: A segment tree is a binary tree where each node represents a range [l, r] of the underlying array and stores an aggregate value (sum, min, max) for that range. Leaf nodes represent single elements. Internal nodes store the aggregate of their two children's ranges. The array representation stores the tree in a 1-indexed array of size 4n (to handle all possible tree shapes when n is not a power of 2). The root is at index 1, the left child of node i is at 2*i, and the right child is at 2*i+1. The parent of node i is at i/2 (integer division). Build: recursively split the range in half (mid = (l+r)/2), build left child for [l, mid] and right child for [mid+1, r], then combine. O(n) build: there are 2n-1 nodes total (n leaves + n-1 internal), each computed once. The 4n size: a complete binary tree for n leaves has at most 4n nodes because the tree has height ceil(log2(n)) and the array needs to accommodate indices up to 2^(ceil(log2(n))+1), which is at most 4n.
lessons.analogy: A segment tree is like a corporate hierarchy where each manager's performance score is the aggregate of their team's scores. The CEO (root) knows the aggregate for the entire company. Each manager knows their department's aggregate. The individual contributors (leaves) are the raw data. Building the tree bottom-up is like computing bonuses from frontline workers up to the CEO without any employee being evaluated more than once.

code_example.explanation: The 4n size guarantee comes from the fact that the segment tree for n elements has height ceil(log2(n)). The last level of a complete binary tree at height h has 2^h nodes, but when n is not a power of 2, the last level is only partially filled. The 4n bound ensures the array is large enough for any n. A tighter bound of 2*2^(ceil(log2(n))) is exact but 4n is simpler to state and always safe.

common_mistakes: Allocating exactly 2n instead of 4n for the tree array — for n that is not a power of 2, the tree needs more than 2n nodes; 4n is the safe upper bound that avoids index out-of-bounds

Using 0-indexed nodes (root at 0) instead of 1-indexed — the 1-indexed representation has the elegant property that left child = 2*i and right child = 2*i+1; 0-indexed requires left = 2*i+1 and right = 2*i+2, which loses the symmetry
Forgetting to combine children in the build function — tree[node] must be set to the combination of tree[2*node] and tree[2*node+1]; forgetting this leaves internal nodes as 0
lessons.interview_relevance: The segment tree build is the foundation for all operations that follow. Interviewers expect candidates to know the 4n size requirement and the 1-indexed array representation. The O(n) build complexity (not O(n log n)) is specifically asked: 'How long does it take to build the segment tree?' The answer requires recognising that each of the 2n-1 nodes is visited exactly once in the recursion.

flashcards.front: Segment tree: what problem does it solve?
flashcards.back: Efficient RANGE QUERIES and POINT/RANGE UPDATES on an array. A balanced binary tree where each node stores the aggregate (sum, min, max, GCD, etc.) of a contiguous subarray. O(log n) per query and update vs O(n) naive scan.

flashcards.front: Segment tree: array representation for a tree with n leaves?
flashcards.back: Use 1-indexed array of size 4n (or 2×next_power_of_2). Node at index i: left child = 2i, right child = 2i+1, parent = i//2. Root = index 1. Leaf nodes correspond to array elements. The 4n bound safely handles all tree sizes.

flashcards.front: Build segment tree: recurrence?
flashcards.back: build(node, start, end): if start==end: tree[node]=arr[start] (leaf). Else: mid=(start+end)//2; build(2*node, start, mid); build(2*node+1, mid+1, end); tree[node] = tree[2*node] + tree[2*node+1] (combine children). O(n) total.

flashcards.front: Segment tree: what is stored at each internal node?
flashcards.back: The AGGREGATE of all array elements in its range [l, r]. For sum queries: sum of arr[l..r]. For min: minimum. For max: maximum. For GCD: GCD of all elements. The aggregate function must be ASSOCIATIVE (order of combining doesn't matter for correctness).

flashcards.front: Segment tree height and build complexity?
flashcards.back: Height = ceil(log₂ n). Total nodes ≤ 4n. Build: visits each of 2n-1 nodes once → O(n). Each leaf takes O(1) to assign; each internal node takes O(1) to combine children → O(n) total.

flashcards.front: Segment tree: what operations does it support natively?
flashcards.back: POINT UPDATE: update a single arr[i] → O(log n). RANGE QUERY: query aggregate over arr[l..r] → O(log n). RANGE UPDATE: with lazy propagation → O(log n). Does NOT support O(log n) sorted insertion (use order-statistic tree for that).

theory_mcq.question: Why does a segment tree array need 4n elements rather than the seemingly sufficient 2n?
options: 4n is an arbitrary safety margin; 2n always works

2n IS sufficient when n is a PERFECT POWER OF 2 (complete binary tree has 2n-1 nodes fitting in indices 1..2n-1); but when n is NOT a power of 2, the tree is INCOMPLETE and some bottom-level nodes require higher indices than 2n-1; for n=5 (height=3), the maximum node index reaches 2^(h+1)-1 = 15 < 4*5=20; the derivation: height h=ceil(log2(n)), max index = 2^(h+1)-1 <= 4n holds for all n; 4n is the universal safe bound covering all cases without needing to compute the exact required size
4n is required because segment trees store both values and parent pointers
The extra 2n space is used by the lazy propagation array in all variants
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's derivation: 'For n not a power of 2: 2^(h+1) <= 4n (by definition of ceil(log2)); For n=5: h=3, 2^4=16 <= 4*5=20 ✓' — 4n is the universal safe bound; for n=9: h=4, 2^5=32 <= 4*9=36 ✓; the extra space is wasted for power-of-2 n but prevents buffer overflows for all other n.

theory_mcq.question: The segment tree build is O(n) because 'each of the 2n-1 nodes is computed exactly once'. Why are there exactly 2n-1 nodes?
options: A balanced binary tree always has exactly n nodes

A FULL BINARY TREE with n LEAF NODES has exactly n-1 INTERNAL NODES (a well-known tree property: in any full binary tree — where every non-leaf has exactly 2 children — internal nodes = leaves - 1); total nodes = n leaves + (n-1) internal = 2n-1; the segment tree is a full binary tree by construction (each non-leaf always has exactly 2 children representing left and right halves); thus 2n-1 nodes are computed during build = O(n) work
The build recurses n times, each taking O(1), giving O(n)
2n-1 nodes come from the 4n array having half its entries unused
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's concept: 'O(n) build: each of the 2n-1 nodes computed exactly once' — the full binary tree property (internal = leaves - 1) gives total = 2n-1; each node computation is O(1) (combine two children); total build work = O(2n-1) = O(n); this is why segment tree build is linear despite the tree having O(n) height.

logic_mcq.question: For segment tree on [1,3,5,7,9,11] (n=6), what is stored at node 1 (root) and why?
options: Root stores 36 (sum of all elements: 1+3+5+7+9+11=36) — confirmed
Root stores 1 (the first element)
Root stores 6 (the count of elements)
Root stores 11 (the maximum element)
logic_mcq.explanation: Confirmed by direct execution: tree[1]=36 for sum segment tree on [1,3,5,7,9,11]; the root covers the entire range [0,5] and stores the aggregate (sum) of all elements; 1+3+5+7+9+11=36; this is the defining property of the root node — it covers the full array range.

logic_mcq.question: In the build recursion, `this.tree[node] = this.tree[2*node] + this.tree[2*node+1]` runs AFTER the two child calls. Why must it come after (not before)?
options: The order is arbitrary; the tree values are the same either way

BOTTOM-UP computation: a node's aggregate depends on its CHILDREN'S aggregates, which in turn depend on THEIR children's aggregates; combining before recursing would use uninitialized values (still 0 from fill(0)); the correct order is: recursively build left subtree → recursively build right subtree → combine results; this is POST-ORDER traversal where the parent's computation happens AFTER both subtrees are fully populated
Combining before recursion would create infinite loops
JavaScript requires sequential array access; out-of-order access causes memory errors
logic_mcq.explanation: Post-order construction is fundamental: the combine step `tree[node] = tree[2*node] + tree[2*node+1]` reads tree[2*node] and tree[2*node+1] which are only correct after their respective subtrees are built; doing this before the recursive calls would combine zeros (initial fill values), not the actual subtree aggregates.

syntax_mcq.question: The tree is 1-indexed (root at index 1) rather than 0-indexed. What is the KEY ADVANTAGE of 1-indexing for tree navigation?
options: 1-indexing prevents off-by-one errors in the mid computation

1-INDEXING enables PURE ARITHMETIC NAVIGATION without conditional checks: left child = 2*node, right child = 2*node+1, parent = Math.floor(node/2); these formulas work perfectly for all valid indices; if the root were at 0: left child = 2*0+1=1, right = 2*0+2=2 — navigation still works but the formulas become 2*node+1 and 2*node+2 (less elegant); 1-indexing makes the Fenwick tree even more natural (operations rely on bit manipulations of 1-indexed positions); 0-indexed would leave index 0 permanently wasted anyway
1-indexing allows using 0 as a sentinel value in the tree array
1-indexing enables O(1) parent lookup without storing parent pointers
syntax_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's concept: 'Array representation: root at index 1, left child = 2*i, right child = 2*i+1' — the 2*i and 2*i+1 formulas work cleanly only when the root is at index 1; with root at 0, formulas become 2*i+1 and 2*i+2 (still correct but less intuitive); the 1-indexed convention is universal for array-represented binary trees.

lessons.title: Point Update And Range Query
lessons.objective: Implement point update and range query on a segment tree in O(log n) each, and trace the path from root to leaf that makes both operations efficient.
concepts: Point update: change a single element, update O(log n) nodes on the root-to-leaf path
Update path: only nodes whose range contains the updated index need updating
Range query: find aggregate over [ql, qr] by combining O(log n) disjoint segments
Query decomposition: split [ql, qr] into at most 2*log(n) stored ranges
O(log n) both: height of tree is log n, each level contributes at most 2 nodes to query
Query base cases: range fully outside [ql,qr] (return identity), fully inside (return stored)
Identity values: 0 for sum, Infinity for min, -Infinity for max
Partial overlap: recurse into both children and combine
lessons.explanation: Point update: to update position i, traverse from root to the leaf for i. At each node, after updating the appropriate child, recompute the node's aggregate from its two children. This updates exactly log(n) nodes (one per level on the path). Range query [ql, qr]: traverse the tree, at each node with range [l, r]: if [l, r] is fully outside [ql, qr], return the identity value (0 for sum, Infinity for min). If [l, r] is fully inside [ql, qr], return tree[node]. Otherwise (partial overlap), recurse into both children and combine the results. At most 2*log(n) nodes are visited because each level of the tree can contribute at most 2 nodes to the result (one from each side of the range boundaries). Both operations are O(log n) = O(tree height).
lessons.analogy: Range query is like asking a company hierarchy 'what is the total performance score for employees 3 through 7?'. You ask each manager: if your entire team is in range, give me your team's aggregate. If your team is completely outside the range, give me nothing. If your team partially overlaps, ask both of your sub-managers. At most two sub-manager responses are needed per level, giving O(log n) managers consulted total.

code_example.explanation: The update path traces exactly from root to the target leaf, updating each node on the way back up (post-order). The query decomposes the range into at most 2 nodes per level of the tree: the leftmost and rightmost segments that partially overlap the query range each contribute at most one node per level. This gives the O(log n) query bound.

common_mistakes: Calling update without propagating changes back up — the recomputation tree[node] = tree[2*node] + tree[2*node+1] must happen on the way back up from the recursive call; without it, internal nodes remain stale

Using the wrong identity value for the aggregate — for range sum, return 0 on fully-outside; for range min, return Infinity; for range max, return -Infinity; using 0 for min would incorrectly report 0 as the minimum when no valid elements are in range

Forgetting the fully-inside check before the partial-overlap recursion — without the fully-inside check (ql <= l && r <= qr), the query recurses all the way to leaves even when an internal node already stores the exact answer
lessons.interview_relevance: Point update and range query are the two fundamental segment tree operations. Range Sum Query - Mutable (#307) is NeetCode 150 and directly tests these. The O(log n) complexity of both operations (versus O(n) for a naive prefix sum update) is specifically asked. Tracing the update path (log n nodes updated) is a common interview question to verify understanding.

flashcards.front: Point update in segment tree: algorithm?
flashcards.back: update(node, start, end, idx, val): if start==end: tree[node]=val; return. mid=(start+end)//2. If idx≤mid: update(2*node, start, mid, idx, val). Else: update(2*node+1, mid+1, end, idx, val). tree[node] = combine(tree[2*node], tree[2*node+1]).

flashcards.front: Range query in segment tree: algorithm?
flashcards.back: query(node, start, end, l, r): if r<start or end<l: return IDENTITY (0 for sum, ∞ for min). If l≤start and end≤r: return tree[node]. mid=(start+end)//2. Return combine(query(2*node,start,mid,l,r), query(2*node+1,mid+1,end,l,r)).

flashcards.front: What is the IDENTITY element for different segment tree operations?
flashcards.back: Sum: 0 (arr[i]+0=arr[i]). Min: +∞. Max: -∞. GCD: 0 (gcd(a,0)=a). AND: all 1s (0xFFFFFFFF). OR: 0. XOR: 0. The identity must satisfy: combine(x, identity) = x for all x.

flashcards.front: Range query: why does it visit O(log n) nodes?
flashcards.back: At each level, the query range [l,r] intersects at most 2 nodes. This is because each node either: (1) is fully within [l,r] → return immediately, (2) is fully outside → return identity, or (3) partially overlaps → recurse on both children. Only 'partial' nodes recurse, and there are O(log n) partial nodes total.

flashcards.front: Segment tree: what aggregate functions are valid?
flashcards.back: Any function that is ASSOCIATIVE: f(a,f(b,c)) = f(f(a,b),c). Sum, min, max, GCD, LCM, AND, OR, XOR, product (careful with overflow), count satisfying a condition, polynomial composition. Does NOT work with average (not associative by itself — need to track sum AND count).

flashcards.front: Difference between point update and range update?
flashcards.back: POINT UPDATE: change one element → update O(log n) nodes on the path from that leaf to root. RANGE UPDATE: change all elements in [l,r] → without lazy propagation: O(n log n) by updating each element. With lazy propagation: O(log n).

quiz.question: What is the identity element for range GCD queries?
options: n (array size)
quiz.explanation: gcd(a, 0) = a for all a > 0. So 0 is the identity for GCD. When a query returns identity (no elements in range), returning 0 is correct since gcd(answer, 0) = answer won't corrupt the combination.

theory_mcq.question: Why does a range query visit at most O(log n) nodes despite potentially spanning many elements?
options: The query prunes entire subtrees when they are fully inside or fully outside the query range

QUERY DECOMPOSITION: at each level of the tree, the query range [ql,qr] can produce at most 2 PARTIAL OVERLAPS (one on the left boundary, one on the right boundary); every other node at that level is either FULLY INSIDE (return stored value immediately) or FULLY OUTSIDE (return identity immediately); with O(log n) levels and at most 2 active nodes per level: at most 2*log(n) nodes are visited total; this O(log n) bound is tight — a query range that spans exactly half the array visits exactly O(log n) nodes
The query uses binary search to find the boundaries, reducing to O(log n)
Range queries are O(log n) because the tree has height log n
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's concept: 'Query decomposition: split [ql,qr] into at most 2*log(n) stored ranges' — the key insight is that per level, at most 2 nodes straddle the query boundary (partial overlap → recurse); all other nodes in the query range are completely inside and returned in O(1); height=log n → at most 2*log(n) nodes visited total.

theory_mcq.question: In `update(idx, val)`, why must `this.tree[node] = this.tree[2*node] + this.tree[2*node+1]` be called on the WAY BACK UP?
options: The combine step on the way back is optional if the leaf was correctly set

BOTTOM-UP PROPAGATION: when a leaf value changes, all ANCESTORS of that leaf have incorrect aggregates; the update descends to the leaf (setting it correctly), then as the recursion returns (back up the path), each ancestor is RECOMPUTED using its two children's current values; all other nodes in the tree are unaffected because only the ancestors of the changed leaf have that leaf in their range; O(log n) recompute steps on the way back = O(log n) total update cost
The combine runs bottom-up to propagate the lazy tag
Without recomputing, the tree structure becomes invalid and future queries fail
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's trace: 'BACK: tree[4]=tree[8]+tree[9]=1+10=11; BACK: tree[2]=tree[4]+tree[5]=11+5=16; BACK: tree[1]=tree[2]+tree[3]=16+27=43' — each ancestor on the leaf-to-root path is recomputed using the now-correct children; only log(n) ancestors exist, giving O(log n) total update.

node1[0,5]: fully inside → return 36
Visits all 11 nodes; sums leaf values 1+3+5=9
node1[0,5]: partial; node2[0,2]: partial; node4[0,1]: inside→4; node5[2,2]: inside→5; returns 4+5=9

lessons.title: Lazy Propagation
lessons.objective: Implement lazy propagation to support range updates in O(log n) by deferring child updates until they are actually needed.
concepts: Range update problem: update all elements in [l, r] by adding delta
Naive: O(n) range update (update each element individually)
Lazy array: stores pending updates not yet pushed to children
Lazy tag: when updating a range, mark internal nodes with pending delta
Push down: before querying or updating children, propagate lazy tags
O(log n) range update + O(log n) range query with lazy propagation
Lazy tag combination: multiple range updates compose additively
Range set vs range add: different lazy tag logic
lessons.explanation: Without lazy propagation, a range update (add delta to all elements in [l, r]) requires visiting all n elements, making it O(n). Lazy propagation defers the update: when updating a range that covers a segment tree node's range entirely, mark the node with a 'lazy tag' (the pending delta) instead of immediately updating all children. The node's stored value is updated to reflect the pending changes, but children are not updated yet. When a future query or update needs to visit a node's children, the lazy tag is 'pushed down' to the children first (propagate the pending update to them and reset the node's lazy tag to 0). This ensures O(log n) range updates because only O(log n) nodes are directly marked with lazy tags. The lazy tag for range-add is additive: if a node already has lazy tag 5 and a new +3 arrives, the combined tag is 8. For range-set (set all elements to a value), the lazy tag is the new value and overwrites any previous lazy tag.
lessons.analogy: Lazy propagation is like a manager who receives a 'give everyone a $100 bonus' instruction for their entire team. Instead of immediately updating every employee's salary, the manager writes '+ $100 pending' on a sticky note (lazy tag) attached to the team roster. Only when someone asks about a specific employee's salary does the manager calculate the actual value and update individual records. This defers work until it is needed, avoiding unnecessary updates for employees whose salaries are never queried.

code_example.explanation: The pushDown is called BEFORE recursing into children in both rangeUpdate and rangeQuery. This ensures that when children are visited, their stored values include all pending lazy updates from ancestors. The order is critical: pushDown, then recurse, then recombine (for updates). Without pushDown before recursing, children would have stale values and queries would return incorrect sums.

common_mistakes: Not calling pushDown before recursing into children — without pushDown, children may have stale values from pending lazy tags of their parent; always pushDown before any recursive child visit

Updating tree[node] without accounting for the range length in lazy propagation — tree[node] stores the sum for the entire range [l, r]; when adding delta to every element, the sum increases by delta * (r-l+1), not just delta
Not resetting lazy[node] to 0 after pushDown — if the lazy tag is not cleared after propagation, future queries will incorrectly apply it again when they push down through this node
lessons.interview_relevance: Lazy propagation is the advanced segment tree technique asked at top-tier companies. It converts range update from O(n) to O(log n). The pushDown mechanism — propagate before recursing — is specifically evaluated. Problems requiring range updates (add to range, set range) all need lazy propagation. This is specifically asked at Google and Uber for problems with both range updates and range queries.

flashcards.front: Lazy propagation: what problem does it solve?
flashcards.back: RANGE UPDATE in O(log n). Without lazy: updating all elements in [l,r] requires O((r-l+1) log n) = O(n log n) worst case. With lazy: defer updates using a 'lazy' array, apply them when needed. Range update + range query both O(log n).

flashcards.front: Lazy propagation: what does the lazy array store?
flashcards.back: Pending updates not yet pushed down to children. lazy[node] = a deferred operation that should be applied to the entire range of this node. When we need to access a node's children, we first PUSH DOWN: apply lazy[node] to both children and clear lazy[node].

flashcards.front: Lazy propagation: pushDown algorithm?
flashcards.back: pushDown(node): if lazy[node] != 0: for child in [2*node, 2*node+1]: tree[child] += lazy[node] × (child_range_size). lazy[child] += lazy[node]. lazy[node] = 0. This applies the deferred update to children before accessing them.

flashcards.front: Lazy propagation: range update for addition?
flashcards.back: updateRange(node, start, end, l, r, val): if range [start,end] fully inside [l,r]: tree[node] += val × (end-start+1); lazy[node] += val; return. pushDown(node). Update left+right children recursively. Recompute tree[node] = combine(children).

flashcards.front: Lazy propagation: when must you pushDown?
flashcards.back: BEFORE accessing children — both in range queries and range updates. Failure to pushDown before a child query/update means the child has stale values that don't reflect the pending lazy update from the parent.

flashcards.front: Lazy propagation: tree[node] formula for range-add?
flashcards.back: tree[node] = sum of elements in [start,end]. After adding val to every element: tree[node] += val × (end-start+1). The lazy[node] += val tracks the per-element addition so children can be updated later.

quiz.question: Lazy propagation: you apply range-add 5 to [0,4] (size 5). tree[root] changes how?
options: tree[root] += 5
tree[root] += 5×5 = 25 (5 elements × value 5)
tree[root] stays the same until pushDown
tree[root] = 5
quiz.explanation: Range add val=5 to range of size 5: tree[root] += 5 × 5 = 25. The root's stored sum increases by the total addition across all elements. lazy[root] += 5 records 'each element in this range has a pending +5'.

quiz.question: When you call rangeQuery([2,4]) on a lazy segment tree and node covering [0,2] has lazy[node]=3, what MUST happen before recursing into its children?
options: Nothing — lazy values are applied during queries
pushDown: apply lazy[node]=3 to both children, clear lazy[node]
Add 3 to the query result
Clear lazy[node] without applying to children
quiz.explanation: pushDown MUST be called before accessing children. Lazy[node]=3 means children have outdated values. Applying to children: each child's tree value += 3 × child_range_size; each child's lazy += 3. Then lazy[node]=0. Only now are children safe to access.

quiz.question: Range-set operation (set all elements in [l,r] to val) with lazy propagation: what's different from range-add?
options: Same implementation — just use val instead of val×size
Range-set needs a different pushDown: tree[child]=val×child_size; lazy[child]=val (overwrite, don't add)
Range-set requires O(n) time
No difference
quiz.explanation: Range-set lazy: when pushing down, the child's entire range is set to val → tree[child] = val × child_size; lazy[child] = val (overwrite). Range-add lazy: tree[child] += lazy[parent] × child_size; lazy[child] += lazy[parent] (accumulate). Different semantics require different pushDown logic.

quiz.question: Lazy propagation: after a range update on [l,r], do you need to recompute tree values on the path to the root?
options: No — lazy values handle everything
Yes — after updating children and clearing lazy, each internal node on the update path recomputes from its children
Only if the query comes in the same function call
Only for the root node
quiz.explanation: After recursively updating children: tree[node] = combine(tree[2*node], tree[2*node+1]). Internal nodes on the update path must be recomputed bottom-up so that future range queries on containing ranges get correct values.

theory_mcq.question: Why is LAZY PROPAGATION needed for range updates, and what problem does naive range update have?
options: Lazy propagation reduces space usage by not storing all intermediate values

NAIVE RANGE UPDATE decomposes into O(n) INDIVIDUAL POINT UPDATES: updating all elements in [l,r] one by one costs O(n log n) per range update; for m range updates, total cost is O(mn log n) — too slow; LAZY PROPAGATION defers the update to child nodes until they are actually accessed: when the current node's range is FULLY INSIDE the update range, mark the node with a LAZY TAG (pending addition) and update the stored aggregate immediately without touching children; children are only updated when a query or further update REQUIRES accessing them (pushed down then)
Naive range update is incorrect; only lazy propagation gives correct results
Lazy propagation is needed only for non-commutative aggregates
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's concept: 'Range update problem: update all elements in [l,r] by adding delta. Naive: O(n) range update (update each element individually)' — lazy propagation achieves O(log n) range update by tagging entire subtrees with pending updates instead of propagating to every leaf; correctness is maintained by pushing down tags before any child access.

theory_mcq.question: In `pushDown(node, l, r)`, why is the SEGMENT SIZE (mid-l+1 and r-mid) multiplied by the lazy tag when updating children's tree values?
options: The size multiplication is an error; lazy tags should be added without multiplying

The lazy tag represents a PER-ELEMENT ADDITION DELTA: if lazy[node]=d, it means every element in node's range should be increased by d; the stored tree[node] is the SUM of all elements in the range; when pushing to a child covering 'len' elements: the child's sum increases by d * len (d added to each of len elements); the child's own lazy tag is incremented by d (to be further propagated when needed); without the multiplication, the sum would be wrong (only d added, not d*len)
The size multiplication handles the case where some elements were already updated
Multiplying by size converts from per-element delta to per-range delta
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's code: `this.tree[2*node] += this.lazy[node] * leftLen` — if lazy[node]=10 and leftLen=3, the left child's sum increases by 30 (10 added to each of 3 elements); the child's lazy tag gets +=10 (propagated per-element for future pushdowns); this correctly decomposes: sum_update = delta * count, tag_update = delta (per-element).

logic_mcq.question: After `rangeUpdate(1, 3, 10)` on [1,2,3,4,5], the array becomes [1,12,13,14,5]. Verify `rangeQuery(0,4)=45` and `rangeQuery(1,3)=39`.
options: 1+12+13+14+5=45 ✓; 12+13+14=39 ✓ — confirmed by direct execution
rangeQuery(0,4)=15+30=45 but rangeQuery(1,3)=30 (only the delta)
rangeQuery(0,4)=40 (misses element 5 which wasn't updated)
rangeQuery(1,3)=36 (3 elements * 10 + original 3+4+5=12)
logic_mcq.explanation: Confirmed by direct execution: rangeQuery(0,4)=45 and rangeQuery(1,3)=39; array after update: [1,2+10,3+10,4+10,5]=[1,12,13,14,5]; total=1+12+13+14+5=45; partial [1..3]=12+13+14=39.

logic_mcq.question: Why is `pushDown` called BEFORE recursing into children in both `rangeUpdate` and `rangeQuery`?
options: pushDown is called after recursion to avoid double counting

CORRECTNESS GUARANTEE: before recursing into a child, any PENDING LAZY TAG on the current node must be propagated to the children; without pushDown first, the children's tree values would be stale (missing the pending update); a query to a child would return an incorrect value, and a further update to a child would be combined with an unaccounted-for parent delta; pushDown before recursion ensures children have CORRECT CURRENT values before any reads or writes; the invariant: if lazy[node]!=0, children's values are wrong by exactly lazy[node]*their_count
pushDown is only needed before rangeQuery, not rangeUpdate
pushDown is called before recursion to reset the lazy array
logic_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's code: `this.pushDown(node, l, r); // propagate before going deeper` in both methods — the lazy invariant: lazy[node] represents a pending per-element delta NOT YET reflected in children; before accessing children, this delta must be pushed; if pushDown were omitted, querying a range that partially overlaps a tagged node would read stale child values.

syntax_mcq.question: When the `rangeUpdate` range FULLY COVERS the current node's range, we do `this.tree[node] += delta * (r-l+1); this.lazy[node] += delta; return`. Why NOT recurse into children here?
options: We must always recurse into children to maintain the tree invariant

The LAZY INSIGHT: when the update range FULLY COVERS [l,r], we can update the node's SUM in O(1) without touching children; delta*len gives the exact sum change; we STORE the per-element delta in lazy[node] for LATER propagation; recursing into children now would be O(n) work (visiting all leaves); by deferring propagation, the range update costs O(log n) total; the children WILL get correct values when pushDown is called before they are next accessed; this deferral is what makes lazy propagation O(log n)
Not recursing saves memory by avoiding stack overflow
Children are not recursed into because they have correct values already
syntax_mcq.explanation: The lazy propagation insight: for a fully-covered node, the sum update is exact and immediate (tree[node] += delta*(r-l+1)), but the per-element update to children is DEFERRED via lazy[node] += delta; deferring avoids the O(n) cost of propagating to all leaves immediately; the correctness guarantee is that pushDown happens before any child access.

lessons.objective: Solve Range Sum Query - Mutable using a segment tree, analyse the tradeoff versus prefix sums and Fenwick trees, and implement the complete NumArray class.
concepts: Range Sum Query Mutable (#307): support both update and range sum query
NumArray class: constructor, update, sumRange methods

Choosing the right tool: prefix sum for read-heavy, segment tree for balanced

lessons.explanation: Range Sum Query - Mutable (#307) asks for a data structure supporting two operations: update(i, val) to change a single element, and sumRange(left, right) to query the sum of a range. Three approaches: (1) Prefix sum array: O(1) query (prefix[right+1] - prefix[left]) but O(n) update (rebuild prefix array). (2) Segment tree: O(log n) both update and query, O(4n) space. (3) Fenwick tree: O(log n) both, O(n) space, simpler code for prefix sums. The segment tree is the right tool when both updates and queries are frequent (mixed workload). For a read-heavy workload (few updates), the prefix sum array's O(1) query is better despite O(n) updates. For write-heavy workloads where only prefix sums are needed (not arbitrary range), the Fenwick tree is simpler and uses less space.
lessons.analogy: Range Sum Query Mutable is like a bank with two operations: change an account balance (update) and compute the total balance for a range of accounts (range sum). A prefix sum array is like a daily summary report: easy to read but expensive to regenerate after any change. A segment tree is like a hierarchical accounting system: both operations are efficient because changes only affect O(log n) summary nodes.

theory_mcq.question: LeetCode #307 offers three approaches: prefix sum, segment tree, and Fenwick tree. When should you choose SEGMENT TREE over FENWICK TREE?
options: Segment tree is always better; Fenwick tree is an inferior alternative

CHOOSE SEGMENT TREE when: (1) the aggregate is NOT a PREFIX SUM (e.g., range minimum, range maximum, range GCD, range XOR) — Fenwick trees natively support only prefix sums; (2) range updates (lazy propagation) are needed — Fenwick trees can support range updates but with more complex logic; CHOOSE FENWICK when: only prefix sums needed and the query range is always [0..r] or computed via subtraction; Fenwick uses less code (~10 lines) and less space (n vs 4n) for the prefix sum case
Segment tree should be used when n is large (>10^5)
Fenwick tree should be used for minimum queries; segment tree for maximum
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's concept: 'Fenwick tree alternative: simpler code, same O(log n) complexity. Practical tradeoff: Fenwick is preferred when only prefix sum is needed' — the segment tree's generality (any associative aggregate, range updates) comes at the cost of more code and 4n space; Fenwick's simplicity and efficiency for prefix sums make it the preferred choice when those constraints fit.

theory_mcq.question: The `(l+r)>>1` operation for computing mid in NumArray. Why use bit-shift instead of `Math.floor((l+r)/2)`?
options: Bit-shift is required because JavaScript doesn't have integer division

For POSITIVE INTEGERS, `(l+r)>>1` is EQUIVALENT to `Math.floor((l+r)/2)` but FASTER: the right bit-shift by 1 divides by 2 and truncates to integer in a single CPU instruction; Math.floor involves floating-point conversion, floor computation, and conversion back to integer — multiple operations; in segment tree implementations with millions of recursive calls, this constant-factor improvement matters; the two forms are identical for non-negative l and r (all valid index ranges); `>>1` is the idiomatic form in competitive programming
>>1 handles negative indices that Math.floor would compute incorrectly
>>1 prevents integer overflow when l+r exceeds 32 bits
theory_mcq.explanation: For non-negative integer indices (all valid segment tree positions), `(l+r)>>1` is exactly equivalent to `Math.floor((l+r)/2)` and is a micro-optimisation; JavaScript engines may optimise both identically in practice; the >>1 form is conventional in performance-sensitive code and explicitly signals 'integer division by 2'.

logic_mcq.question: The complexity table shows: prefix sum has O(1) query but O(n) update. WHY is prefix sum update O(n)?
options: Prefix sum array has n entries, each taking O(1) to compute — so O(n) total

When a SINGLE ELEMENT changes, ALL PREFIX SUMS starting from that position change: if nums[i] changes by delta, then prefix[i], prefix[i+1], ..., prefix[n-1] all change by delta (since prefix[j] = sum(nums[0..j])); updating all n-i affected prefix sums requires O(n) time; this is the fundamental tradeoff — storing prefix sums enables O(1) range queries but makes updates O(n); segment trees and Fenwick trees break this tradeoff by accepting O(log n) for both
Prefix sum update rebuilds the entire array from scratch
Only the prefix sums at even indices need updating, giving O(n/2)≈O(n)
logic_mcq.explanation: The O(n) update cost of prefix sums follows from their definition: prefix[j] = sum(nums[0..j]) includes nums[i] for all j >= i; changing nums[i] invalidates all prefix[j] for j in [i, n-1] — that's n-i entries requiring recomputation; in the worst case (i=0), all n prefix sums need updating.

syntax_mcq.question: In `NumArray`, the build method is named `_build` (with underscore). What JavaScript convention does this signal?
options: _build is a JavaScript reserved keyword that forces private method syntax

UNDERSCORE PREFIX is a CONVENTIONAL SIGNAL that the method is PRIVATE or INTERNAL — not part of the public interface; JavaScript doesn't enforce true private methods by default (unlike Python or Java); `_build` tells users of the NumArray class that this method is an implementation detail, not meant to be called from outside; modern JavaScript uses `#build` (with hash) for true private fields/methods; the underscore convention predates the `#` syntax and remains common in codebases for compatibility
_build is called differently than build due to the leading underscore
Methods starting with _ are automatically memoised by JavaScript engines
syntax_mcq.explanation: The underscore prefix is a longstanding JavaScript convention (inherited from Python) signalling 'this is an internal implementation method'; it's not enforced by the language but communicates developer intent; modern JavaScript uses `#name` for actual private class fields/methods; in the NumArray context, `_build` is called only from the constructor and should not be called by external code.

lessons.title: Binary Indexed Tree — Fenwick Tree
lessons.objective: Implement a Fenwick Tree (Binary Indexed Tree) for prefix sums in O(log n) per operation using the elegant lowbit operation, and understand why it is simpler than a segment tree for prefix sum problems.
concepts: Fenwick tree: compact array where bit[i] stores sum of a specific range
lowbit(i) = i & (-i): isolates the lowest set bit of i
update(i, delta): add delta to position i, propagate to ancestors
prefix query(i): sum from 1 to i, follow parent chain
Range query [l, r]: query(r) - query(l-1)
O(log n) both operations: lowbit removes bits, log n steps max
1-indexed: Fenwick trees work naturally with 1-indexed arrays
Why simpler than segment tree: no explicit tree structure, ~10 lines total
lessons.explanation: A Fenwick tree (Binary Indexed Tree) is a compact data structure for prefix sums that achieves O(log n) per update and query. The bit array bit[i] stores the sum of a range of elements determined by i's binary representation: bit[i] covers elements from i-lowbit(i)+1 to i, where lowbit(i) = i & (-i) gives the value of the lowest set bit of i. For example, bit[6] (binary 110, lowbit=2) covers elements 5 and 6. Update(i, delta): add delta to bit[i], then move to the next responsible node by adding lowbit(i). This propagates upward through all ancestors. Query(i): sum from position 1 to i by adding bit[i], then moving to the previous responsible node by subtracting lowbit(i). This aggregates downward through all relevant buckets. Both operations take at most log(n) steps because each step either gains or loses a set bit. The Fenwick tree's elegance: the entire implementation is ~10 lines with no explicit tree structure or recursive calls.
lessons.analogy: The Fenwick tree is like a system of overlapping team leads where each lead is responsible for a specific crew size determined by their ID's binary representation. Team lead 6 (binary 110) is responsible for the last 2 employees before them. Team lead 8 (binary 1000) is responsible for the last 8. When you update an employee's performance, you update their direct lead and all leads who cover that employee. When you query the total for employees 1 through i, you collect exactly the right set of non-overlapping lead reports.

code_example.explanation: The alternating direction in update (add lowbit) vs query (subtract lowbit) is the key to the Fenwick tree's correctness. Update moves toward larger indices (toward the root in a conceptual tree), collecting all nodes responsible for covering position i. Query moves toward smaller indices (toward position 0), collecting non-overlapping prefix segments that together cover [1, i]. The two operations are inverses of each other in the index traversal direction.

common_mistakes: Using 0-indexed arrays with Fenwick trees — Fenwick trees are inherently 1-indexed because lowbit(0) = 0 causing an infinite loop in update/query; always convert 0-indexed input to 1-indexed (i+1) when calling Fenwick operations
Confusing the direction of index traversal — update adds lowbit (moves toward larger indices); query subtracts lowbit (moves toward smaller indices); reversing them gives wrong answers

Not implementing O(n) build (using n point updates instead) — building with n calls to update is O(n log n); there is an O(n) build using the parent-child relationship but O(n log n) is acceptable for most interviews
lessons.interview_relevance: The Fenwick tree is the preferred data structure for prefix sum with updates in competitive programming and is increasingly asked at top-tier companies. Count of Smaller Numbers After Self (#315, NeetCode 150) uses a Fenwick tree or merge sort for the optimal O(n log n) solution. The lowbit trick (i & (-i)) is specifically evaluated: 'Explain what i & (-i) computes and why it is useful.'

flashcards.front: Fenwick Tree (BIT): key operation — lowbit?
flashcards.back: lowbit(i) = i & (-i). The lowest set bit of i. Example: i=6=110₂, -6=...11111010₂ (two's complement), 6&(-6)=000...010=2. This operation determines how much of the array each BIT node covers.

flashcards.front: BIT: what does bit[i] store?
flashcards.back: bit[i] stores the sum of arr[i - lowbit(i) + 1 .. i]. The range length = lowbit(i). bit[4]=arr[1..4] (lowbit(4)=4). bit[6]=arr[5..6] (lowbit(6)=2). bit[5]=arr[5..5] (lowbit(5)=1).

flashcards.front: BIT: prefix sum query prefix(r) algorithm?
flashcards.back: result = 0. While r > 0: result += bit[r]. r -= lowbit(r) (r &= r-1). Return result. Each step removes the lowest set bit → O(log n) iterations. Answer = sum of arr[1..r].

flashcards.front: BIT: point update at index i algorithm?
flashcards.back: While i ≤ n: bit[i] += delta. i += lowbit(i). Each step moves to the next BIT node that covers index i. O(log n) updates. This propagates the change to all BIT nodes that include arr[i] in their range.

flashcards.front: BIT range query [l, r]?
flashcards.back: prefix(r) - prefix(l-1). BIT natively supports prefix sums. Range sum [l,r] = prefix(r) - prefix(l-1). This is always O(log n) per range query.

flashcards.front: BIT vs segment tree: concrete code complexity difference?
flashcards.back: BIT: ~10 lines total (init, update, query). Segment tree: ~40-50 lines (build, update, query with recursion). BIT is strictly simpler for prefix-sum queries. Tradeoff: BIT CANNOT handle arbitrary range queries (like range minimum), only prefix sums.

theory_mcq.question: What does `lowbit(i) = i & (-i)` compute and why does it work?
options: lowbit computes the highest set bit of i

lowbit(i) isolates the LOWEST SET BIT of i: -i in two's complement is ~i+1 (invert all bits then add 1); this sets all bits BELOW the lowest set bit of i to 1 and all bits AT AND ABOVE it to 0 (except the lowest set bit itself which stays 1); i & (-i) then extracts only the lowest set bit position; example: i=6=0110, -i=1010 (two's complement), i&(-i)=0010=2 (bit 1) ✓; i=8=1000, -i=1000, i&(-i)=1000=8 (bit 3) ✓
lowbit computes floor(log2(i))
lowbit is equivalent to i modulo 2
theory_mcq.explanation: Confirmed by direct execution: lowbit(6)=2, lowbit(8)=8; the two's complement explanation: -i = ~i + 1 flips all bits above the lowest set bit and sets that bit to 1 (via carry); i & (-i) then zeros everything except the shared lowest set bit; this operation is the foundation of both Fenwick update (add lowbit to move up) and query (subtract lowbit to move to prefix parent).

theory_mcq.question: In Fenwick update, `i += this.lowbit(i)` moves to the NEXT node that bit[i] CONTRIBUTES TO. In query, `i -= this.lowbit(i)` moves to the PREVIOUS PREFIX BUCKET. Why are these directions opposite?
options: The directions are arbitrary; both operations could use either direction

The Fenwick tree has an ASYMMETRIC structure: bit[i] stores the sum of a range ENDING AT i with length lowbit(i); QUERY traverses backward: to compute prefix[i]=sum(1..i), we need bit[i] (covers i-lowbit(i)+1 to i), then bit[i-lowbit(i)] (covers its own range), etc. — moving LEFT (subtracting lowbit) collects non-overlapping ranges; UPDATE traverses forward: when element i changes, all ANCESTORS whose range CONTAINS i must be updated — i contributes to bit[j] whenever j's range includes i, which happens for j = i, i+lowbit(i), i+lowbit(i)+lowbit(i+lowbit(i)), etc. — moving RIGHT (adding lowbit)
The opposite directions are needed to avoid infinite loops
Update uses addition to prevent index 0 from being accessed
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's trace: 'TRACE update(6): i=6→bit[6]+=delta, i=8→bit[8]+=delta; TRACE query(6): i=6→sum+=bit[6], i=4→sum+=bit[4], i=0 stop' — the divergent directions are inherent to the Fenwick tree's structure: update propagates upward (to all ancestors), query aggregates leftward (collecting disjoint prefix ranges); these are two different tree traversals on the same underlying structure.

syntax_mcq.question: The Fenwick tree is 1-indexed but `buildFenwick(nums)` converts 0-indexed nums using `ft.update(i+1, nums[i])`. What would happen if `ft.update(i, nums[i])` were used (no +1)?
options: No difference — Fenwick trees can be either 0-indexed or 1-indexed

Using `ft.update(i, ...)` without +1: when i=0, the update is called with position 0; in the Fenwick update loop `while(i<=this.n)`, starting at i=0: i+=lowbit(0)=0 (since 0 & (-0) = 0 & 0 = 0) — the loop NEVER TERMINATES (infinite loop); the Fenwick tree REQUIRES 1-indexing because lowbit(0)=0 would cause the update loop to get stuck at i=0 forever; the 1-indexed convention is not just convention — it's a correctness requirement for the i+=lowbit(i) termination to work
0-indexed Fenwick trees work correctly; the +1 is a coding style preference
ft.update(0,...) would update position n (the last position) due to wrap-around
syntax_mcq.explanation: Critical correctness issue: lowbit(0) = 0 & (-0) = 0 & 0 = 0; the update loop `i += lowbit(i)` with i=0 gives i=0+0=0 → infinite loop; the query loop `i -= lowbit(i)` with i=0 gives i=0-0=0 → infinite loop; 1-indexing ensures all valid indices have non-zero lowbits, guaranteeing termination; this is why Fenwick trees are ALWAYS 1-indexed.

lessons.title: Range Query Problem Thinking
lessons.objective: Select the correct range query data structure for any problem based on supported operations, and map all Module 2 NeetCode 150 problems to their patterns.
concepts: Decision tree: point update vs range update, prefix query vs range query
Prefix sum: O(1) query O(n) update, static or read-heavy arrays
Fenwick tree: O(log n) both, prefix sums only, simpler code
Segment tree: O(log n) both, arbitrary range aggregates, flexible
Lazy segment tree: range updates + range queries in O(log n)
Sparse table: O(n log n) build, O(1) query for idempotent functions (min/max)
Module 2 NeetCode 150 problems mapped
Skills unlocked: Segment Tree, Fenwick Tree, Lazy Propagation
lessons.explanation: Range query data structures solve the fundamental problem: given an array with frequent updates and range queries, how do you answer range queries efficiently after updates? The decision tree: (1) No updates (static array): use prefix sums for O(1) range sum, or sparse table for O(1) range min/max. (2) Point updates, prefix sums only: Fenwick tree. (3) Point updates, arbitrary range aggregates (sum, min, max, GCD): segment tree. (4) Range updates + range queries: lazy segment tree. (5) Very large n with many distinct values: coordinate compression before any of the above. Sparse table: a different structure for O(1) range minimum/maximum queries (RMQ) that works only on static arrays. Preprocessing takes O(n log n). Queries are O(1) using the overlap property of min/max (idempotent): sparse[i][j] = min(sparse[i][j-1], sparse[i + 2^(j-1)][j-1]).
lessons.analogy: Range query data structure selection is like choosing the right filing system for a library. A sorted bookshelf (prefix sum) is perfect for reading but reorganising takes forever. A hierarchical catalogue (segment tree) allows both finding and updating books efficiently. A simple ledger (Fenwick tree) is perfect if you only need cumulative totals. Choosing the wrong filing system makes one operation fast and the other prohibitively slow.

code_example.explanation: The sparse table uses the overlap property of idempotent operations: for range minimum, min(arr[l..r]) = min(sparse[l][k], sparse[r-2^k+1][k]) where k = floor(log2(r-l+1)). The two windows of size 2^k overlap, which is fine for min/max because min(x, x) = x (idempotent). This overlap trick is what enables O(1) queries but makes sparse table inapplicable to sum queries (sum(x, x) != sum of the range).

common_mistakes: Using a segment tree when a Fenwick tree suffices — if the problem only requires prefix sums with point updates, Fenwick tree is simpler and more memory-efficient; reserve segment trees for general range aggregates
Applying sparse table to a dynamic array (with updates) — sparse table is a static structure; any update requires O(n log n) rebuild; only use for completely static arrays

Not recognising when coordinate compression is needed — when values in the problem are large (up to 10^9) but the number of distinct values is small (up to n), compress coordinates to [1..n] before applying range structures
lessons.interview_relevance: Module 2 covers 2 NeetCode 150 problems (Range Sum Query Mutable and Count of Smaller Numbers After Self) plus the foundational data structures (segment tree, Fenwick tree, lazy propagation, sparse table) that underpin competitive programming and senior engineering interviews. The decision tree for selecting the right structure is specifically evaluated in system design DSA questions.

flashcards.front: Range query problem decision: when to use segment tree vs BIT vs sparse table?
flashcards.back: SPARSE TABLE: O(n log n) build, O(1) query, NO updates — for static arrays with min/max queries. BIT: O(log n) update+query, sum only — for dynamic arrays needing prefix sums. SEGMENT TREE: O(log n) update+query, any associative aggregate — for dynamic arrays with complex aggregates or range updates.

flashcards.front: Coordinate compression: when is it needed with BIT?
flashcards.back: When values are large (up to 10^9) but count is small (n ≤ 10^5). Map values to rank in [1,n] to fit in a BIT of size n. Example: [100, 3, 50, 3] → ranks [3, 1, 2, 1] (sorted unique: [3,50,100]). BIT of size 3 instead of 10^9.

flashcards.front: Offline vs online range queries: what's the difference?
flashcards.back: OFFLINE: all queries known upfront. Can process in sorted order, use divide-and-conquer or sorted event sweeps. ONLINE: queries arrive one at a time; answer each before the next arrives. Segment tree and BIT support online; some offline-only techniques (Mo's algorithm) cannot.

flashcards.front: Segment tree on strings: what operations are possible?
flashcards.back: Each node stores an aggregate over substring characters. Example: count distinct characters in range (node stores a bitmask of chars). XOR/AND of character frequencies. Hash of substring. The aggregate function must still be associative and computable from children.

flashcards.front: 2D range queries: two approaches?
flashcards.back: 2D SEGMENT TREE: O(n² log² n) space, O(log² n) query. 2D BINARY INDEXED TREE: O(n²) space, O(log² n) update+query. For n ≤ 10³: both feasible. For n ≤ 10^4: may exceed memory. Alternative: 1D segment tree where each node has a sorted list of values (merge sort tree) for 2D queries.

flashcards.front: Mo's algorithm: when is it useful?
flashcards.back: OFFLINE range queries where: (1) adding/removing one element from the window is O(1) or O(√n), and (2) all queries are given upfront. Sort queries by (l//√n, r). Total operations: O((n+q)√n). Useful when no data structure handles the specific aggregate cleanly.

quiz.question: Static array, n=10^5, only range minimum queries, no updates. Best approach?
options: Segment tree O(n) build, O(log n) query
Sparse table O(n log n) build, O(1) query — optimal for static arrays
BIT — always the best for range queries
Naive O(n) per query
quiz.explanation: No updates → static array → sparse table. O(n log n) build, O(1) query using overlap property of powers of 2. No segment tree needed since updates never happen.

quiz.question: Count of smaller numbers to the right: arr=[5,2,6,1]. For element 5, how many elements to its right are smaller?
options: 2 (both 2 and 1)
2 — only 2 and 1 are < 5
quiz.explanation: To the right of 5: [2,6,1]. Smaller than 5: 2 and 1. Count = 2. The answer array would be [2,1,1,0].

quiz.question: BIT with coordinate compression for [5,2,6,1] (Count Smaller After Self). Coordinate compression maps these to?
options: [5,2,6,1] (unchanged)
quiz.explanation: Sorted unique values: [1,2,5,6]. Ranks: 1→1, 2→2, 5→3, 6→4. Array [5,2,6,1] → ranks [3,2,4,1]. BIT of size 4 instead of size 6 (original max value).

quiz.question: Mo's algorithm processes queries in which order?
options: Left endpoint ascending
Blocks of size √n: sort by (l//√n, r) — alternating r direction for each block
Random order for better cache performance
Right endpoint descending
quiz.explanation: Mo's ordering: primary sort by block (l//√n), secondary by r (ascending in even blocks, descending in odd blocks — 'hilbert curve' optimisation). This minimises total pointer movement to O((n+q)√n).

RANGE QUERY DATA STRUCTURE SELECTION:

Criteria          Sparse Table    BIT          Segment Tree
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Range update      ✗              ✗            O(log n)*
Range min/max     O(1) query     ✗ (sum only) O(log n)

theory_mcq.question: The SPARSE TABLE achieves O(1) query but requires the aggregate function to be IDEMPOTENT. What does idempotent mean and why is it required?
options: Idempotent means the function returns the same value for the same input (like identity)

IDEMPOTENT means f(x, x) = x — applying the function to the SAME VALUE twice gives the same result; min(x,x)=x and max(x,x)=x are idempotent; sum is NOT idempotent (x+x=2x≠x); sparse table achieves O(1) query by using TWO OVERLAPPING POWER-OF-2 RANGES that together cover [l,r]; since the ranges overlap, some elements are counted TWICE; for idempotent functions (min/max), counting twice is harmless; for sum, counting an element twice gives the wrong answer — which is why sparse table doesn't support sum queries with O(1) time
Idempotent means the function is commutative (order doesn't matter)
Idempotent functions are required for O(n log n) build time
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's concept: 'Sparse table: O(n log n) build, O(1) query for idempotent functions (min/max)' — the O(1) query trick: find k=floor(log2(r-l+1)), then min(table[l][k], table[r-(1<<k)+1][k]); the two ranges [l, l+2^k-1] and [r-2^k+1, r] overlap but min(a,min(a,b))=min(a,b) by idempotency; if sum were used: sum(a, sum(a,b)) = 2a+b ≠ a+b (wrong).

theory_mcq.question: For the decision guide: given 'range min queries, NO updates', which structure is optimal and why?
options: Segment tree — it handles all cases including static arrays

SPARSE TABLE: when there are NO UPDATES, the array is STATIC and the sparse table's O(n log n) build cost is paid once; queries are O(1) per query — faster than segment tree's O(log n); for q queries: sparse table costs O(n log n + q) vs segment tree's O(n + q log n); when q is large, sparse table wins decisively; for dynamic arrays (with updates), sparse table cannot efficiently update (O(n log n) per update makes it impractical) — segment tree or lazy segment tree is required
Fenwick tree — it handles all range queries in O(log n)
Prefix sum — it has O(1) query for all aggregate types
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's decision guide: 'if !hasUpdates && (queryType==='min'||queryType==='max') return Sparse Table O(n log n) build, O(1) query' — the No-Updates + min/max combination makes sparse table the clear winner; its O(1) per query advantage over segment tree's O(log n) is decisive for query-heavy workloads; static arrays are the prerequisite since sparse table rebuild is prohibitively expensive.

logic_mcq.question: For `sparseTableQuery(st, 2, 5)` on [3,1,4,1,5,9,2,6], the result is 1. Verify using the range [2..5]=[4,1,5,9].
options: Range [2..5] = [4,1,5,9]; min = 1 ✓; k=floor(log2(4))=2; table[2][2]=min(arr[2..5])=1; table[5-4+1=2][2] also covers position 2; result=min(1,1)=1 ✓
sparseTableQuery(2,5) returns 4 (the first element in the range)
The result is 9 (the maximum of [4,1,5,9])
sparseTableQuery cannot handle ranges of length 4; it returns -1
logic_mcq.explanation: Confirmed by direct execution: sparseTableQuery(st,2,5)=1; range [2..5]=[4,1,5,9]; min=1; k=floor(log2(4))=2; the two overlapping ranges: [2..5] (table[2][2]) and [2..5] (table[5-4+1][2]=table[2][2]); both return 1; min(1,1)=1 ✓.

logic_mcq.question: Module 2 has 2 NC150 problems (#307 and #315). Problem #315 'Count of Smaller Numbers After Self' uses 'Fenwick + coordinate compression'. What does coordinate compression enable here?
options: Coordinate compression sorts the array to enable binary search

COORDINATE COMPRESSION maps potentially large values (e.g., nums[i] up to 10^4) to SMALL INDICES (1..n) so the Fenwick tree's size is O(n) rather than O(max_value); for #315: to count smaller numbers to the right of each element, process right-to-left; compress values to rank 1..n; for each element at rank r, query(r-1) gives count of smaller already-seen elements; update(r, 1) registers the current element; without compression, the Fenwick tree would need size 10^4+1 even for n=5 elements
Coordinate compression converts the 2D problem to 1D
Compression is needed only when elements are negative
logic_mcq.explanation: Coordinate compression for Fenwick trees: map actual values to ranks 1..n; this bounds the Fenwick tree size to O(n) regardless of value magnitude; for #315, process right-to-left with a Fenwick tree tracking seen values by rank; query(rank-1) = count of elements already seen with rank < current rank = elements to the RIGHT (already processed) that are SMALLER; this gives O(n log n) solution vs O(n²) naive.

syntax_mcq.question: In `sparseTableQuery`, `const k = Math.floor(Math.log2(r - l + 1))` computes k once for O(1) query. Why is precomputing log values (not computing at query time) important for production?
options: Math.log2 is not available in all JavaScript environments

Math.log2 is a FLOATING-POINT OPERATION costing multiple CPU cycles; for O(1) queries to be practically fast, the log computation must not be the bottleneck; in production sparse tables with millions of queries, precomputing a LOG TABLE (log2[i] for i=1..n) converts the log lookup to O(1) array access (faster than computing Math.log2 each time); the lesson's implementation computes Math.log2 per query for simplicity; a production implementation would precompute: `const logTable = Array.from({length:n+1}, (_,i)=>Math.floor(Math.log2(i||1)))`
Math.log2 returns floating-point; the integer conversion via Math.floor is O(n)
Precomputing log values enables parallel processing of multiple queries
syntax_mcq.explanation: Production sparse table optimisation: precompute `log[i] = floor(log2(i))` for i=1..n as an O(n) array; query lookup then costs O(1) integer array access instead of O(1) floating-point log computation; for 10^8 queries, the constant factor matters; the lesson's Math.log2 approach is pedagogically clear and functionally O(1), but production code precomputes the log table.

module_summary.difficulty: Hard — segment trees and BITs require careful index arithmetic; lazy propagation is the most complex data structure implementation in the curriculum
core_patterns: Segment tree: 1-indexed array of size 4n; left=2i, right=2i+1; build O(n) postorder
Range query: return IDENTITY when range doesn't intersect; return node when fully inside; else split at mid
Point update: recurse to leaf, update leaf, recompute ancestors bottom-up
Lazy propagation: store pending update in lazy[]; pushDown before accessing children in ANY operation
Range update: if fully inside, apply to node + update lazy, return; else pushDown + recurse + recompute
BIT prefix query: sum bit[i], then i -= lowbit(i) until i=0
BIT point update: bit[i] += delta, then i += lowbit(i) until i>n
lowbit(i) = i & (-i) — lowest set bit of i
Coordinate compression: map large values to ranks in [1,n] for BIT over value space
unlocks_modules: Competitive programming: segment tree beats, persistent segment trees
module_summary.spaced_review_target: Re-implement BIT from scratch (10 lines) before attempting the harder problems

module_summary.key_implementation_rule: The single most common bug in lazy segment trees: forgetting to call pushDown BEFORE accessing children — in BOTH the query AND the update function. This causes reading stale child values when lazy updates haven't been propagated. Always: before recursing into children, call pushDown(current_node).
